pages.title: Creating Strings and String Literals
pages.content:
# Strings in JavaScript

A string represents a sequence of 16-bit Unicode characters used to store and manipulate text.

### Ways to Declare Strings
- **Single quotes**: `'Hello World'`
- **Double quotes**: `"Hello World"`
- **Template literals**: ``Hello World``

There is no semantic difference between single and double quotes. Template literals introduce multi-line support and string interpolation with `${expression}`.

```javascript
const language = "JavaScript";
const message = `Welcome to ${language} programming!`;
console.log(message);
```

callout.title: String Length
callout.text: The .length property returns the total number of UTF-16 code units in the string. It is a read-only property.

codeCard.code:
const greeting = "Hello, Developer!";
console.log("Length:", greeting.length); // 18
console.log("First character:", greeting[0]); // 'H'
console.log("Using charAt:", greeting.charAt(7)); // 'D'

checkpoint.question: Which property returns the number of characters in a string?
checkpoint.explanation: In JavaScript, string.length is a property (not a method) that returns the length of the string.

pages.title: String Immutability and Indexing
pages.content:
# String Immutability and Indexing

In JavaScript, strings are **immutable**. Once created, their individual characters cannot be modified in-place.

### Character Access
You can access characters using bracket notation (`str[index]`) or `str.charAt(index)` (zero-indexed).

```javascript
let word = "Java";
word[0] = "K"; // Silently fails in sloppy mode, TypeError in strict mode!
console.log(word); // Still "Java"
```

To change a string, you must construct and return a new string.

callout.title: Strings Cannot Be Mutated
callout.text: Any string method like toUpperCase() or replace() returns a new string and does NOT mutate the original variable.

checkpoint.question: What happens if you run str[0] = 'X' on an existing string in JavaScript?
options: The first character is changed to 'X'
The string remains unchanged because strings are immutable
The string is converted to an array
A compile error is always thrown
checkpoint.explanation: JavaScript strings are immutable; modifying an index using bracket notation has no effect and the original string remains intact.

pages.title: Essential String Methods (slice, replace, includes)
pages.content:
# Common String Methods

JavaScript provides extensive built-in methods on string instances:

### Extraction Methods
- **`slice(start, end)`**: Extracts a section from `start` up to (but not including) `end`. Supports negative indexes.
- **`substring(start, end)`**: Similar to slice, but treats negative indexes as `0`.

### Inspection & Search
- **`includes(sub)`**: Returns `true` if `sub` is found within the string.
- **`indexOf(sub)`**: Returns the first index where `sub` occurs, or `-1` if not found.
- **`startsWith(sub)`** and **`endsWith(sub)`**: Boolean prefix/suffix tests.

### Modification & Trimming
- **`replace(search, replaceWith)`**: Replaces the first match (or all matches with regex `/g`).
- **`replaceAll(search, replaceWith)`**: Replaces all occurrences.
- **`trim()`**: Removes whitespace from both ends.

callout.title: Prefer slice() over substr()
callout.text: slice(start, end) is the modern standard method. substr() is deprecated in modern ECMAScript.

checkpoint.question: Which method checks whether a string contains a specified substring and returns a boolean?
checkpoint.explanation: In modern JavaScript, string.includes(substring) returns true if the substring is present, otherwise false.

pages.title: Template Literals and Multi-line Strings
pages.content:
# Template Literals in ES6

Template literals use backticks (`` ` ``) instead of quotes and offer powerful features:

### 1. Expression Interpolation
You can evaluate any valid JavaScript expression inside `${...}`:
```javascript
const a = 10, b = 20;
console.log(`Sum: ${a + b}`); // "Sum: 30"
```

### 2. Multi-Line Strings
Prior to ES6, multi-line strings required concatenation or `\n`. Template literals preserve newlines naturally:
```javascript
const report = `
  Invoice #101
  Total: $500
`;
```

### 3. Tagged Templates
Functions can tag template literals to parse and sanitize string inputs (used by libraries like styled-components).

callout.title: Expressions Inside ${}
callout.text: Any expression can go inside ${}: function calls, ternary operators, math calculations, and nested template literals.

checkpoint.question: What syntax is used to embed an expression inside a JavaScript template literal?
checkpoint.explanation: In ES6 template literals, expressions are embedded using the ${expression} syntax.

practiceProblems.title: Concatenation
practiceProblems.description:
The '+' sign can be used between  `strings`  to add them together to make a new  `string`.\
This is called  **`concatenation`**.\
For eg - 
```javascript
var x = "Good";
var y = "Work";
console.log(x + y);   //output: GoodWork
```
**Note**: You can add spaces between words by using an empty " " with a space inside or by providing a space at the end of a word. \
For eg - 
```javascript
var x = "Good";
var y = "Work";
console.log(x + " " + y);   // output: Good Work
```

- Declare two variables  **`x`**  and  **`y`**
- Assign the values  **`Hello`**  to variable  **`x`**  and  **`World`**  to variable  **`y`**.
- Output  **`x`**  and  **`y`**  to the console. Don't forget to add a space in between them. \
Your output will be  **`Hello World`**

practiceProblems.title: Outputting Characters from a String
practiceProblems.description:
In a string, characters are indexed from left to right. For instance, in a string named **hello** the first character is at index 0, while the last is at index str.length-1 (i.e., at the 4th index).

We use the concept of  `indexing`  which means every character in a  `string`  corresponds to a number called the  `index number`
        
                   0 1 2 3 4 5 6 7  - index number
         for eg - "C o d e C h e f"

Following are some of the ways we can access a specific character in a string in javascript: 

1. using square brackets notation **[ ]**
```javascript
var str = 'hello';
console.log(str[1]); // e
```
When we try to access a character whose index is equal to or larger than the string length, the square brackets [] return **undefined**.

```javascript
var str = 'string';
console.log(str[999]); // undefined
```
2. using **charAt()** method
This method will return the character at a specified index in a string. The method takes in a parameter, an integer that represents the index of the character to be returned. The syntax for usage is **string.charAt(index)**.

```javascript
var str = 'string';
console.log(str.charAt(0)); // s
//If no character is found, the method returns an empty string.
var str = 'string';
console.log(str.charAt(999)); // ''
```


**Note** 
- Indexing always starts from  **`0`**  when going left to right. 
- So the first character of a  `string str`  is  `s[0]` , the second is  `s[1]` , and so on.

### Task
Write a program which does the following
- Create a  `string`  variable  **`word`**  and assign the text  **`Programming`**  to it
- Print the characters  **`o`**  and  **`r`**  from the string  **`word`**  in separate lines using the syntax defined above

practiceProblems.title: Changing Characters in a String
practiceProblems.description:
In JavaScript,  `strings`  are immutable, which means you cannot directly update or change a character in a  `string`. 
For example
```javascript
var name = "Chaf";
name[2] = 'e'; // nothing changes.
console.log(name); // Chaf
```
If you run the above program, you will still get the same string `Chaf`.

However, you can create a new  `string`  with the desired changes.\
Here's an example of how you can replace the character 
```javascript
var name = "Chaf"
var newName = name.replace('a', 'e');
console.log(newName); // Chef
```
**Note:** If there are multiple occurrences of the substring you're trying to replace within the original string, the replace() method in JavaScript by default only replaces the first occurrence of the substring.
For eg:
```javascript
var name = "Chafaf";
var newName = name.replace('a', 'e');
console.log(newName); // Chefaf
```

### Task
Write a program which does the following
- Given a  `string`  variable  **`word`** which has value  **`"Ocygen"`**.
- You now want to fix the typo in the given string.
- Use the syntax explained above to replace  `'c'`  with  `'x'`  in a new variable  `newWord`
- Output the updated  **`newWord`**  to console

practiceProblems.title: String slicing
practiceProblems.description:
String slicing in JavaScript involves extracting a portion of a string by specifying the starting and ending indices. 

You can achieve this using the `slice()` method. Here are a few examples:

#### `slice()` method:

```javascript
var originalString = "Hello, World!";
var slicedString = originalString.slice(7, 12);

console.log(slicedString); // World
```


#### Omitting the End Index:

If you omit the end index, the slice will go until the end of the string:

```javascript
let originalString = "Hello, World!";
let slicedString = originalString.slice(7);

console.log(slicedString); // World!
```

In this case, it extracts from index 7 to the end of the string.

#### Negative Indices:

You can use negative indices to count from the end of the string:

```javascript
let originalString = "Hello, World!";
let slicedString = originalString.slice(-6, -1);

console.log(slicedString); // World
```

This extracts from the 6th character from the end to the 1st character from the end.


### Task
- Declare a string variable **str**
- Assign the value **String** to it
- Use string slicing to print **ring** to the console.

practiceProblems.description:
We have learned so many new things about strings in this lesson.

You should now know how to:
1. Concatenate or join two strings using the + operator.
2. Find the length of a string using the length property of the string.
3. Output and replace characters from a string.
5. Get a substring of any string.

In the next lesson, we will solve exercises on these topics to deeply understand how they work and also how to apply them when needed.

questions.explanation: indexOf() returns -1 if the search value is not found in the calling string.

questions.explanation: toUpperCase() returns the calling string value converted to uppercase.

questions.question: What is the output of 'foo'.repeat(3)?

questions.question: How do you remove whitespace from both the beginning and end of a string?

questions.explanation: replace() with a string pattern replaces only the first occurrence, returning 'bonana'.

questions.question: Which method splits a string into an array of substrings based on a separator?
questions.explanation: split(separator) divides a String into an ordered list of substrings and returns them in an array.

questions.question: What does 'JavaScript'.startsWith('Java') return?
